ttps://ew.com/article/1998/12/11/black-lieutenant-syndrome/

Black Lieutenant Syndrome (sometimes abbreviated BLS) is a term to describe a recurring casting pattern in American police procedurals and cop dramas.

Since at least the 1970s, television producers frequently cast Black actors as the ranking authority figures—typically lieutenants, captains, or squad commanders—over the main detective teams. These characters often serve primarily as bureaucratic or supervisory figures: they assign cases, bark orders, mediate disputes among the detectives, absorb criticism from higher-ups downtown, and provide occasional moral or institutional commentary. However, they usually receive far less personal dramatic development, screen time for action or personal storylines, or narrative centrality compared with the (predominantly white) street-level detectives who drive most of the plots, investigations, and character arcs

The pattern was seen as a convenient way for shows to signal diversity and deflect accusations of tokenism. By making “the boss” Black, producers could claim meaningful representation (“Sure, there’s only one Black regular, but they’re the one in charge”) without centering a Black character as the primary protagonist who solves cases, faces the main dangers, or drives romantic/personal subplots. Critics and some producers at the time viewed it as a limited, often underwritten role that prioritized appearances of progressiveness over fully realized characters.

Here is just a small sample: 

Classic / 1990s-era examples

Law & Order — Lt. Anita Van Buren (S. Epatha Merkerson), long-running squad commander. 

NYPD Blue — Lt. Arthur Fancy (James McDaniel), precinct/squad boss. 

Homicide: Life on the Street — Lt. Al Giardello (Yaphet Kotto), shift/squad commander. 

In the Heat of the Night — Capt. Virgil Tibbs (Howard Rollins); later Chief Hampton Forbes (Carl Weathers).

Martial Law — Capt. Winship (Tom Wright). 

The X-Files — Assistant Director (James Pickens Jr.) as a higher-up boss for the agents. 

2000s–2010s examples

The Wire — Cedric Daniels (Lance Reddick) rises through multiple command ranks (lieutenant → major → colonel → commissioner). 

Castle — Capt. Roy Montgomery (Ruben Santiago-Hudson).

Brooklyn Nine-Nine — Capt. Raymond Holt (Andre Braugher) as precinct commander; Sgt. Terry Jeffords (Terry Crews) as a key leader/supervisor. 

S.W.A.T. (2017–) — Sgt. Daniel “Hondo” Harrelson (Shemar Moore) as team leader of the 20-Squad. 

The Rookie — Sgt./Lt. Wade Grey (Richard T. Jones) as watch commander / ranking supervisor at the Mid-Wilshire station.

NCIS — Director Leon Vance (Rocky Carroll), overall agency head/boss.

9-1-1 — Athena Grant (Angela Bassett), who holds sergeant and higher field/leadership roles.

More recent examples

East New York — Capt./Deputy Inspector Regina Haywood (Amanda Warren) as precinct commander.
